我把这本书命名为《新原理：社会科学的数学原理》，英文主标题采用拉丁语形式 Nova Principia。这个名字表达的是一个研究方向：从存在与变化、构造与演化的基本问题出发，寻找能够连接自然科学、人的认知与社会合作的共同语言，并把它落实到可以试验、可以修正的制度与技术中。它不是宣布我已经完成了一套与牛顿体系相当的定理，也不意味着人的需要与价值能够被一条公式包办。正因为这个目标尚未完成，书中既要大胆提出联系，也要把需要证明、需要实验和需要共同选择的部分说清楚。

## 相对性、认知参考系与社会科学的数学表达

### 我们从什么地方观察世界

当两个人站在同一条街道的两端，一个人说汽车正在靠近，另一个人说汽车正在远离，他们未必有谁说错了。问题在于，汽车正在靠近谁，又正在远离谁？如果把各自所在的位置、观察的方向和测量的时刻说清楚，原本看起来互相冲突的描述，就可以放到同一个关系中理解。

但是，如果一个人说汽车已经撞到了行人，另一个人说没有发生碰撞，那么仅仅说“大家的参考系不同”，并不能解决这个分歧。我们需要核对现场、时间、影像和其他证据。前一种差异可能来自描述方式，后一种差异涉及对同一事件的判断。能够区分这两种情况，才是把相对性引入认识问题的起点。

参考系既有物理上的内容，也需要数学上的表达。观测者使用什么仪器、怎样同步时钟、相对于什么测量运动，是物理问题；用什么坐标标记事件、怎样在不同表达之间转换，是数学问题。在狭义相对论中，相对性原理要求物理规律在惯性参考系之间保持一致，而不是说任何观察、任何测量和任何猜测都同样正确。爱因斯坦的工作通过明确测量与转换规则，保留了可以共同检验的物理关系。[爱因斯坦1905年论文](https://courses.physics.illinois.edu/phys225/sp2026/Einstein1905.pdf)

我想进一步追问的是：从物理到化学、生物，再到人的认知与社会，我们能不能同样学会分清，哪些差异来自对象本身，哪些差异来自处境，哪些差异只是来自描述对象的方式？

这种追问不要求不同领域使用同一套公式。为化学计算选定一个能量参考值，与一个生物在特定环境中能否生存，不是同一种相对性。前者可以涉及表示上的约定，后者涉及条件改变以后实际结果的改变。一个性状在一种环境中有利，在另一种环境中不利，不能被说成只是换了坐标，现实中的生存条件也发生了变化。把这些区别保留下来，跨领域的联系才有意义。

### 社会科学应该建立在什么底座上

社会科学的体系应该与自然科学体系建立在同一个理论底座上，而不是有什么上帝创造的独立于宇宙演化规则之外的所谓意识灵魂之类超自然因素影响的额外规则和元素。人的身体、感觉、记忆、语言和合作，并没有在宇宙之外另起一个世界。我们不应因为对象变成了人，就把最需要解释的现象变成不能追问的例外。

这是本书采取的研究立场：尽可能用可检验的机制解释现象，同时允许解释本身被新证据改变。它不需要先裁决每个人的全部宗教信仰，也不意味着一套物理方程就能直接代替心理学、经济学和制度研究。层级越高，关系越复杂，我们越需要找到适合这一层级的对象、变量、边界和测量方法。

在我看来，当前社会科学的一些基础争论，仍让人联想到牛顿体系之前的自然哲学的状态，急需底层基本概念和数学原理层面的统一底座。而且这个底座应该是自然科学底座的自然延伸。人们掌握了大量经验，也提出了许多解释，但对概念的含义、不同解释怎样连接，以及怎样共同检查结论，仍有很大的分歧。我希望寻找的，是一个更能够连接这些研究的底座。

这种类比不能抹去已经存在的成果。社会科学早已使用统计、博弈论、因果分析和网络模型，也已经形成了许多可以检验的研究。问题不是从零开始宣布所有旧知识都无效，而是让彼此分散的知识更容易说明各自的假设、尺度和适用条件，进而共同构造更有效的社会机制。

可以把这个方向理解为寻找社会科学中的坐标与参考系：怎样描述一个人的处境，怎样比较不同人的判断，怎样识别共同事实，又怎样追踪互动之后对象本身的改变。它借鉴笛卡尔坐标、牛顿参考系和爱因斯坦相对论所体现的研究精神，而不是声称已经发现了可以把物理相对论直接搬到社会中的变换公式。

### 语义空间带来了什么新的可能

AI领域的发展，使硅基计算设备能够完成越来越多过去由人类智能完成的任务。这个事实为一种认识提供了更加具体的基础：语言、知识处理和部分推理活动，可以通过可研究、可构造的机制来实现；人类社会中的问题，也可以进一步尝试用数学模型和科学实验来认识。

尤其是大模型，使大规模语言材料的语义关系能够以高维表示进入计算。我们可以把不同说法放到一起比较，寻找相近与相异之处，追踪某个概念在不同语境中的变化，再据此帮助构造和修正社会模型。这是我希望把认知空间纳入研究的重要技术条件。

但这里有两个边界需要说明。第一，语言与认知的数学建模并不是从今天的大模型才开始。例如，1997年的潜在语义分析研究，已经用高维表示研究词语、文本与知识获取。第二，一个模型能够表示语言材料之间的关系，不等于已经完整测量了一个人的意识。没有表达出来的经验、身体感受、情绪与动机，不能因为模型给出了一个向量，就被当成已经全部掌握。[Landauer与Dumais的潜在语义分析研究](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/350/2008/readings/Landauer-Dumais.pdf)

因此，我所说的认知空间，首先应当从可以操作的范围开始：人们自愿提供的言论、解释、选择以及相关处境。它们可以被记录和分析，形成关于某些认知关系的近似模型。模型中的维度是否有意义，测量能否重复，换一个模型或换一种语言以后结论是否仍成立，都需要检验。不能把某个模型内部的一条轴，直接宣布为全人类共同的“正义轴”或“文明程度轴”。

### 每个人的认知坐标，都有形成的条件

人类的世界观、认识论、政治倾向、道德观念和认知体系，在语义空间的不同认知与行为维度上，具有不同的位置、倾向和变化方向。这些差异与每个人的经历、所处环境、能够取得的信息以及受到的影响有关。一个人的认识不是凭空出现的，也不能仅仅因为它属于自己，就获得绝对正确的地位。

在这一意义上，我认为，人类这种以自身经验为出发点的认知参考系，可以放到更广泛的演化图景中考察。一个能够感知和行动的系统，首先需要区分什么与自己有关，什么会影响自己的持续存在，再在互动中逐步扩展认识。至于这是不是每一个可进化、可涌现系统都具有的基本性质，仍需要针对不同系统分别研究，不能仅凭人的经验便推广到整个宇宙。

如果把现在的AI语言大模型看作人类语言知识的一种高维语义表示，那么基于这个认知空间的语言和行动，就像物理时空中的运动一样，可以帮助我们想象认知如何在互动中变化。这里借用的是运动与变化的比喻，并没有预先假定两者服从相同的方程。每个人的认知参照不同，可能因此产生隔阂，也可能通过解释建立信任；这些不同参照系中的人类个体之间的互动行为在文明和社会层级这个更高的参照系中会形成更复杂的结构和性质。新的结构反过来影响个体，使他们接触到不同的信息，形成新的习惯与判断。

这里同时发生着两件事：我们在改变对世界的描述，也在通过行动改变世界。一个人把另一群人理解为敌人，可能因此拒绝交流；拒绝交流又使双方更难纠正误解，进而改变了真实的合作关系。社会模型因此不能只保存静态的观点坐标，还必须记录信息、行为、资源与规则怎样随时间变化。这也就是本书后面从语义对象走向文明运行时的原因。

### 承认相对性，不等于取消事实与责任

那么，既然认知的出发点不同，是不是就没有任何对错与好坏可言？

我想反对的，是把自己的认知坐标系直接当成绝对正确的标准，将一切与自己不一致的事物都看作错误，再把不同的人解释为天生的敌人或恶魔。但是，从“不能用自己的位置代替普遍标准”，不能推出“任何事实判断都一样可靠，任何行为都一样可以接受”。

一个人在什么环境中形成某种恐惧，可以被理解；他据此作出的事实判断，仍然可能被证据纠正。他为什么伤害别人，可以有因果解释；已经发生的伤害，仍然需要停止、救济和追责。理解行为的形成条件，与允许行为继续发生，是不同的问题。

比如，两个人争论一项公共设施。一个人看见交通变得方便，另一个人承受噪音、搬迁或生活成本。不能只把前者称为进步，把后者称为自私；也不能只把前者称为掠夺，把后者称为正义。先把便利给了谁、代价由谁承担、还有什么替代方案记录清楚，分歧才会从身份对立转变为可以研究的问题。

但即使信息已经充分，双方仍可能面对真实的利益冲突。一份有限的资源，不能仅靠把两个人的话互相翻译，就同时满足所有要求。我们还需要共同商定规则、比较方案、保护基本权利并安排补偿。相对性帮助我们识别分歧的结构，不能代替分配问题本身的解决。

### 让道德判断回到可以讨论的事实与规则

人类的一切社会层面的认知和行为现象，都应该像自然现象一样，进入可观察、可研究、可记录、可分析的范围，并在测量条件允许时尝试量化和建模。我们不应通过神秘化、神圣化、妖魔化与情绪化的标签，阻止对这些现象的进一步研究。

你可以在文字作品中，在诗歌小说里，情绪化、神圣化或妖魔化自然界的对象，比如温柔的风，柔顺的小草，神圣的光，恶魔般的黑暗。这些表达具有文学与情感的价值。但是，在自然科学的理论研究和技术实践中，不能用“黑暗是恶魔”来代替对光的传播的解释。人类社会的对象同样需要如此对待：不能因为先把某个人或某种制度称作神圣，就免除其接受证据检查的责任；也不能因为先把对方称作邪恶，就认为无需再理解其形成原因。

这不要求人们没有情绪，也不要求公共表达失去修辞。恐惧、愤怒、同情和希望，本来就是需要理解的真实现象。需要避免的，是让这些感受直接充当未经检验的因果结论，或者成为剥夺别人解释、申辩和参与机会的理由。政治实践关系到真实的人，尤其不能用一群人的神圣感，代替另一群人的同意与安全。

我们仍然可以坚持不伤害、平等参与与保护自主等基本规则。只是这些规则要明确说明适用范围、发生冲突时怎样处理、由谁解释、怎样修正，而不能把制定者的身份当成最后的证明。一个人即使不同意我的全部世界观，也可以和我共同检验某个事实、遵守一项合作协议。这样形成的共同基础，比要求所有人先拥有同一个内心世界，更接近可以实践的合作。

### 怎样把数学词语变成可以使用的结构

向量、张量、对象与态射、对偶、对称、不动点、最大化和最小化，可以为研究提供工具。但把这些词语排列在一起，不会自动产生一门新的科学。每使用一个概念，都要说明它指向什么，允许什么操作，操作前后有什么关系，以及怎样发现它不适用。

|数学概念|在社会研究中可以尝试的表达|必须回答的问题|
|---|---|---|
|维度、向量|在指定任务中，用多个量描述需要、资源、判断或风险|每个量怎样测量，单位是什么，哪些内容被遗漏；向量不是一个人的全部|
|张量|在定义了空间及变换规则以后，表达具有相应变换性质的多维关系|不能把任何多维表格都称为具有同样数学性质的张量|
|对象、态射、范畴|把知识对象、状态或协议作为对象，把允许的转换作为态射|转换能否组合，是否有恒等转换，组合是否满足所声明的规则|
|对称性、相对性|检查更换名称、单位或表达以后，相关判断是否保持一致|哪些变化只是重新表达，哪些已经改变处境、权利或事实|
|对偶性、两种侧面|研究两种结构化描述之间的对应，或知识与智能、数据与程序之间的联系|严格的数学对偶需要定义；两个相互关联的概念并不自动构成对偶定理|
|不动点、均衡、极值|描述某种更新不再改变状态、策略互为回应，或指标在约束下达到极值|更新规则、收益与约束分别是什么；稳定、有效、公平与最优不能互相替代|

比如，为了帮助两个合作小组澄清分歧，我们可以先约定一个任务，把他们自愿提交的材料与相关情境记为 $h_i,c_i$，用一个明确版本的表示方法 $E_i$，得到 $x_i=E_i(h_i,c_i)$。这里的 $x_i$ 只是这项任务中的表示，不是对人的定型，更不是测得了灵魂的坐标。

然后，尝试构造一个解释关系 $T_{ij}$，把甲的说法转述到乙可以理解的语言中。检验的方法可以很朴素：甲是否认为原意得到保留，乙是否能够更准确地复述，双方是否能就可核对的事实提出相同的检查。如果只能做到部分对应，就记录缺失；如果翻译改变了含义，就保留反例。不能因为写出了 $T_{ij}$，便假定它必然可逆、无损，或具有某种几何变换的全部性质。

接着，还要询问：理解改善以后，真实合作有没有改善？有时误解消除了，方案就能调整；有时双方已经充分理解，仍然因为资源不足而无法同时实现愿望。后一种情况需要进入协商与分配，而不是继续增加模型参数，假装所有冲突都是语义问题。

### 从认知参考系走向共同构造

我所希望建立的，不是一个替所有人规定正确坐标的中心，而是一种让不同认知可以相互解释、共同核验并继续演化的机制。Merkle-DAG可以保留原话、来源、条件、版本与修改关系，使某个模型给出的解释不会悄悄覆盖当事人的表达。模型会变，解释会变，过去的原话和分歧仍然可以被找回。

共同记录也不意味着一切私人经验都必须公开。能够用经过授权的摘要、局部计算或有限证据解决的问题，就不必索取完整生活。认知模型越有能力，越需要明确谁有权使用它，使用的目的是什么，当事人怎样纠正和退出。

从这里再看合作、冲突和社会结构，就会出现一个更具体的问题：我们能否让拥有不同知识、需要和偏好的人，在保留差异的同时，建立可以共同信任的行动规则？相对性让我们放下把自己当成绝对中心的习惯，共同核验使我们不至于迷失在彼此不能对话的世界中，而制度的构造，则要把这种理解转化为能够持续的合作。这三步连接起来，才是我希望寻找的社会科学数学底座。

### 对齐首先需要回答：与谁对齐

前面讨论认知参考系时，我们已经看到，人们可以在同一个世界中，拥有不同的信息、需要和判断。现在，把AI放进这个持续博弈的系统，就需要追问一个经常被省略的问题：当我们说“让AI与人类对齐”时，这里的“人类”，究竟指谁？

人工智能与大模型的对齐（AI Alignment），通常被解释为使人工智能系统的输出、行为与人类的价值观、意图及社会规范保持一致的过程。对于聊天模型，一个容易理解的目标，就是让模型从“只会续写文字的基座”变成“有用、诚实、无害的助手”。利用人的示范与反馈改进模型，是其中一类实际研究路径。但把一个模型训练得更符合某些用户或评审者的期望，与解决全社会的价值分歧，还隔着许多问题。[利用人类反馈训练语言模型的研究](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)

从这个定义出发，结合人类文明内部，不同民族、不同政权、不同阶层的人们，其价值观、意图、政治规则和社会规范并不完全一致的客观事实，就会很自然地发现：在人类社会博弈游戏中，每个具有创造和控制AI能力的玩家——某个政权、某个社会阶层、某个公司，或某个人——所研发和掌握的那个对自己“有用、诚实、无害的助手”，在这个游戏中，都有可能成为其他对手玩家眼中，对自己“可怕和有害的”游戏对手的帮凶。

一个AI可以非常准确地执行委托人的要求，同时把损失转嫁给没有参与委托的人。比如，一套系统能够提高企业的谈判效率，但如果成功的定义只包括企业收益，就可能把劳动者的处境当成可以忽略的外部条件。问题不一定出在AI违背了主人，反而可能出在它过于有效地完成了一个没有纳入所有受影响者的目标。

因此，局部对齐不能直接等同于整体安全。要评价一个系统，除了看它是否听懂了委托人的话，还要看委托人能授权什么、其他人的哪些权益不能被越过、发生影响以后谁能提出异议。这已经超出了单个聊天助手怎样回答问题，进入共同生活的制度结构。

### 能力失衡与力量对峙，为什么都需要共同规则

随着AI能力提高，以及研究、编程与实验等环节中自动化能力的扩展，掌握这些工具的玩家可能更快地扩大行动能力。如果不同玩家获取算力、数据、人才和基础设施的条件差距很大，AI也可能进一步放大这种差距。

我们需要重视短时间内发生巨大变化的风险，但不能在没有具体任务与证据时，给出“几个月必然造成成百上千倍能力差距”的统一比例。设计新机制，并不需要先证明某一个夸张数字；只要某些能力的增长明显快于共同约束与纠错的增长，就已经值得认真对待。

如果发展不平衡，造成一家独大的局面，优势玩家可能认为，利用AI赋能来压制其他各方，比与他们平等协商更容易。这时，若收益只从优势一方的局部范围计算，其他人的生命、自主、未来的信任与整个文明失去的创造力，都可能被排除在账本之外。

但是，这不意味着暴力镇压必然是收益最高、成本最低的策略。它会引起抵抗、破坏信息质量、损害合作，并产生长期的不确定性。前面关于理性说服与自愿试点的讨论，正是在寻找另一种选择。这里需要警惕的是：缺少共同约束时，局部的评价方式可能奖励损害整体的行为，而不是宣布一切领先者注定采用暴力。

如果发展相对平衡，形成几方对峙的局面，也不能因此宣布问题已经解决。彼此的不信任、信息交互的不充分，以及行动速度过快，可能使各方在没有什么主观的强烈恶意的情况下，随便一个小念头，或者一点点小误会，就引发文明毁灭的危险。甚至各方最初只是想避免自己落后，也可能不断采取刺激对方恐惧的行动。冷战核对峙所引起的共同忧虑，帮助我们理解这种结构性危险，但AI的作用方式与核武器并不相同，具体风险还要具体分析。

能力失衡与力量对峙，因而是两种需要研究的风险路径，并非穷尽未来的两种必然结局。双方可以建立沟通、核验、限制外部伤害与共同处理事故的规则，也可以在保留竞争和差异的同时，减少不可挽回的升级。真正需要改变的，是把相互伤害当成取得安全的唯一办法。

### 双手各挥一把链子锤的文明

之前举的那个小孩挥舞链子锤的例子，在上面的关于对齐的演绎中，有了具体可能的场景。把中美之间带有对抗性的AI竞赛作为一个例子，它就像一个具有左右两个大脑的智能生物，左右双手各挥一个链子锤，但是左右大脑之间缺乏有效的对齐机制，导致其挥舞链子锤的控制，无法有效地协同。

左边的大脑认为，右边的锤子越来越快，自己必须更快，才能避免受伤；右边的大脑作出同样的判断。于是，两只手都在提高力量和速度，却没有共同检查轨迹。每一边都以保护自己为理由，最终却可能因为两个锤子之间的碰撞和缠绕，导致武器失控伤及自己。

这个比喻突出的是相互依赖与协调不足，并不是说一个国家只有一种意志，也不是说世界只有中美两个参与者。两国内部有不同的人与组织，其他国家和广大普通人也会承受影响。正因为受影响者远多于少数决策中心，共同规则才不能只由挥锤的人私下决定。

更好的出路，不是先把另一半身体打断，也不是让一个大脑永远奴役另一个，而是让双方可以验证：什么行动会产生共同危险，哪些信息有必要共享，怎样发现误判，怎样及时停止，怎样使纠错不被解释为认输。力量仍然可以增长，但增长要伴随协调能力的提高。

### 人与人的对齐，人与AI的对齐

甚至从全局的宏观层面上，人类有时把自己作为一个整体，将AI视为这个博弈游戏中的另一个对手，担心AI一旦具有了自我意识，就会从人类的助手，变成奴役甚至毁灭人类的暴君。前文已经说明，自我意识、目标和行为可靠性不能直接画上等号；同样，人类也不是一个早已拥有统一目标、统一行为的玩家。

在我看来，真正不能再回避的，是全人类各个组织和个体之间的对齐：怎样让各自的价值观、意图与规范，在实际输出和行为中受到共同规则的约束，使任何一方追求自己的目标时，不轻易破坏其他人的基本生存与自主条件。

这不要求所有人拥有相同的审美、信仰、职业偏好或人生目标。需要对齐的，首先是合作的元规则，以及承诺和行动之间的关系。我们可以不同意同一种生活最好，却同意不通过胁迫使对方接受；可以竞争解决同一个问题，却共同保留结果和失败的记录，让别人继续检验；可以对方案有异议，却仍然保护提出异议的人的基本权利。

在这个意义上，人的制度对齐改善了，人与AI的对齐就有了更扎实的共同基础。谁有权提出目标，哪些人会受影响，授权能否撤回，代价由谁承担，争议如何处理，不再全部隐藏在模型的委托关系背后。合作AI研究也把人与机器之间、多个智能体之间如何改善共同处境作为明确的研究方向。[合作AI的开放问题](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.08630)

但共同基础并不会自动消除技术问题。目标可能被错误表达，模型可能误解反馈，系统可能在新环境中失效；即使参与者真诚合作，也仍需要检验系统能否按授权行动，能否被停止，能否在出错时恢复。人与人的制度协调，以及人与AI的技术对齐，需要相互促进、并行推进，不能等一方彻底完成之后，另一方才开始。

### 对齐作为不动点，需要怎样的数学表达

我提出“对齐也是一种不动点”，想表达的是：当各方持续观察、行动、反馈和修正规则时，能否形成一种不会不断把彼此推向伤害的协调关系？

要让这个想法进入数学，首先要明确，谁是不动的对象，什么是作用在它上面的变换。一个回报函数通常把状态和行动映射为某种评价，例如 $r_i(s,a)$。它的输入与输出未必属于同一个空间，因此，不能直接把“回报函数的不动点”当成已经定义好的概念。

我们可以把各方的评价规则、行动策略和合作协议，合在一起记为 $z$，再定义一个根据证据与反馈修正这些内容的更新规则 $F_e$，其中 $e$ 表示暂时固定的环境条件。于是，讨论的对象可以写成：

$$
F_e:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z},\qquad z_{t+1}=F_e(z_t),\qquad F_e(z^*)=z^*.
$$

此时，$z^*$ 才是这个更新规则下的不动点。如果我们特别关心回报评价的修正，也可以把一组评价函数记为 $R$，在同一个函数空间中定义更新算子 $U$，讨论 $U(R^*)=R^*$。这是一种有待具体构造和检验的建模方式，并没有证明现实社会一定存在这样的点，更没有证明从任意起点都能到达它。

而且，不动点本身没有公平的含义。一套制度可能因为弱者无法发声而长期不变，也可能因为错误信息被反复确认而保持稳定。我们要寻找的，必须是满足基本权利、可质疑、可修正等条件的协调状态，并检验它遭受扰动以后会怎样。稳定性、存在性和正当性，是不同的要求。

纳什均衡说明在给定其他人策略时，个体是否还愿意单方面改变；帕累托最优检查能否在不使其他人变差的情况下继续改善某个人；最大化与最小化则必须先说明指标、约束与代价。它们各自回答一类问题，不能因为都涉及“不再改变”，就被当成同一个结论。以牙还牙更是一种具体回应策略，不是天然通往最优状态的定理。

现实世界还会出现新对象、新技术与新需要，环境 $e$ 也会变化。因此，更实际的目标可能是一条持续满足共同约束、允许局部试验并及时修正的演化路径，而不是把文明永远锁定在一个点上。对齐应当使共同进化能够继续，而不是让一套评价函数永远不能改变。

### 从人类与AI，延伸到共同生存的生态

进一步说，我们要做的是人类与AI共同组成的新文明体，与整个地球乃至所进入的宇宙环境之间的协调。这是我所说的对齐的更长远目标。

人类已经面临过核武器造成大范围毁灭的风险，也正在面对现代生产生活累积造成的气候变化。关于后者，IPCC第六次评估综合报告明确指出，人类活动已经造成全球变暖。如果不在最宏观的层面上检查文明行动的外部影响，AI赋能也可能让旧有的破坏模式变得更快、更大。[IPCC综合报告](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/)

这里的生态对齐，不是说地球或宇宙有一套等着我们读取的统一意志，也不是说存在一个已经给定的宇宙回报函数。它要求我们把能源、物质循环、生态承受能力，以及其他生命与未来世代受到的影响，真正纳入决策和反馈。某项行动在账面上收益很高，如果把无法恢复的损害留给没有发言机会的人，就不能轻易称为文明整体的进步。

由此，对齐不再只是模型在一次对话中是否给出令人满意的回答。它同时涉及个人与组织之间、人与AI之间，以及文明与其生存条件之间的关系。不同层面的检验不能互相代替，却必须连接起来：目标怎样产生，信息怎样取得，权力怎样受到约束，结果怎样记录，错误怎样修复。后面所讨论的公共知识、动态权重与制度自我进化，就是试图为这条完整链条提供可以逐步实践的结构。

### 相对性怎样避免变成不能检验的万能解释

把参考系的思想延伸到认知与社会，具有提出新问题的价值，但目前并没有一套已经得到验证的“社会相对论”。需要分别检查：我们是在重新表达同一事实，还是改变了环境条件；是在发现不同的人如何理解世界，还是在提出应该怎样共同生活的规则。三个问题有关联，却不能由一个答案包办。

语义向量是依据材料、训练方法与任务形成的表示，不是对意识的完整测量。一个可行的小实验，应当让愿意参与的双方先独立解释同一项分歧，再比较普通转述与模型辅助转述，检查误解是否减少、原意是否保留，并在未参与构造的材料上继续检验。还要记录模型没有帮助、误判或抹去真实利益冲突的情况。向量距离更近，本身不能作为更公平、更信任或更安全的证明。

同样，把认知差异叫作曲率，把信任叫作平行移动，把观点转换叫作函子，如果没有定义对象、关系与可检验的结构，只能算启发性的比喻。数学名称不会替一个尚未构造的模型提供证明。真正需要争取的是让不同表达之间的关系可以被检查，而不是把人安置在一个看起来精确、实际却无法反驳的坐标中。

### 对齐的固定状态与持续修正，分别需要什么证据

将对齐写为更新算子的不动点，是一个研究提议。它需要给出状态空间、允许的更新、环境假设、参与者的权利与成功标准。关于存在、收敛、扰动后的恢复，以及能否满足共同约束，需要分别证明或实验检验。一个长期稳定的支配结构，就是“稳定所以良好”这一推断的反例。

可以从小规模的资源合作开始：比较只追求各自局部得分的代理，与使用共同损害限制、公开承诺和纠错程序的代理，在信息误差、能力不平衡和资源变化下的表现。记录收益分布、受损次数、修复时间、退出是否有效与总成本，保留不合作或串谋等反例。模拟结果只能帮助选择进一步试验的方向，不能直接证明全球社会可以安全照搬。

人类制度协调有助于明确AI的目标与授权，但不能代替技术安全的检验；生态约束也不能只用人类参与者暂时同意的得分来代表。新原理所追求的共同底座，应当使这些缺口更加清楚，使失败更容易暴露，使修正能够继续发生，而不是用一个统一名称提前宣布所有问题已经解决。

I call this book Nova Principia: Mathematical Principles of Social Science. The title names a direction of inquiry: beginning with existence and change, construction and evolution, I seek a language that can connect natural science, human cognition, and social cooperation, then inform institutions and technologies that can be tested and revised. It does not announce a completed system of theorems comparable to Newton's, or suggest that one equation can settle human needs and values. Because the project remains unfinished, the book must both propose connections boldly and distinguish what requires proof, what requires experiments, and what requires shared choices.

## Relativity, Cognitive Frames, and a Mathematical Language for Social Science

### Where are we observing from?

Two people stand at opposite ends of a street. One says a car is approaching; the other says it is moving away. Neither need be mistaken. The question is: approaching whom, and moving away from whom? Once we specify their positions, directions of observation, and times of measurement, apparently conflicting descriptions can become parts of a single account.

Suppose, however, that one person says the car has struck a pedestrian and the other says no collision occurred. Saying that everyone has a different frame of reference will not settle this disagreement. We need to examine the scene, timing, recordings, and other evidence. The first difference may concern how an event is described; the second concerns what happened. Bringing relativity into questions of knowledge begins with distinguishing the two.

A frame of reference has physical content and requires mathematical expression. Which instruments observers use, how they synchronize clocks, and what they measure motion relative to are physical questions. How they label events and translate between descriptions are mathematical questions. In special relativity, the principle of relativity requires consistency of physical laws across inertial frames. It does not make every observation, measurement, or guess equally correct. Einstein made measurement and transformation rules explicit so that physical relationships could remain open to shared tests. [Einstein's 1905 paper](https://courses.physics.illinois.edu/phys225/sp2026/Einstein1905.pdf)

I want to take the question further. Across physics, chemistry, biology, cognition, and society, can we learn to distinguish differences in objects themselves from differences in circumstances, and both from differences in the way objects are described?

This does not require every field to use the same equations. Choosing a reference value for an energy calculation in chemistry is not the same kind of relativity as an organism's ability to survive in a particular environment. The former may involve a representational convention; the latter concerns a change in actual outcomes when conditions change. A trait that helps in one environment may hinder in another. That is more than a change of coordinates: the conditions of survival have changed. Connections across fields become useful when these distinctions remain visible.

### What foundations should social science share?

Social science and natural science should rest on the same underlying foundations, rather than invoke additional rules or supernatural elements—a God-given consciousness or soul standing outside the universe's evolutionary processes. Our bodies, sensations, memories, language, and cooperation do not inhabit a separate world outside the universe. When our subject becomes human, we should not turn the very phenomena that need explanation into exceptions we cannot investigate.

The research stance of this book is to explain phenomena through mechanisms that can be tested, while allowing new evidence to change those explanations. It does not require settling everyone's religious beliefs in advance. Nor does it mean that a physical equation can replace psychology, economics, or institutional research. As relationships become more complex at higher levels of organization, we need objects, variables, boundaries, and methods of measurement suited to those levels.

Some foundational disputes in social science remind me of natural philosophy before Newton, with an urgent need for a common basis of fundamental concepts and mathematical principles. That basis should extend the foundations of natural science. There is abundant experience and there are many explanations, yet profound disagreements remain over what concepts mean, how explanations connect, and how conclusions can be assessed together. I hope to find foundations that make these bodies of inquiry more connected.

The analogy must not erase existing achievements. Social scientists already use statistics, game theory, causal analysis, and network models, and have established many testable findings. The task is not to start from nothing by declaring previous knowledge worthless. It is to help separate bodies of knowledge state their assumptions, scales, and limits more clearly, so they can contribute to better social arrangements.

We might understand this project as a search for coordinates and reference frames in social science. How do we describe a person's circumstances, compare different judgments, identify shared facts, and trace changes brought about by interaction? The inspiration comes from the investigative spirit of Cartesian coordinates, Newtonian frames, and Einstein's relativity. It is not a claim to have discovered equations that transfer physical relativity directly into society.

### What semantic spaces make possible

AI has enabled computing devices built from silicon to perform a growing range of tasks once performed by human intelligence. This gives concrete support to an important possibility: language, knowledge processing, and some forms of reasoning can be realized through mechanisms we can study and construct. Problems in human society can likewise be approached through further mathematical modeling and scientific experiments.

Large language models, in particular, allow semantic relationships in extensive bodies of language to be represented computationally in high-dimensional spaces. We can compare different expressions, identify similarities and differences, and follow changes in a concept across contexts. Those representations may help us construct and revise social models. This is an important technical condition for the study of cognition that I have in mind.

Two distinctions matter here. First, mathematical models of language and cognition did not begin with today's large models. Research on latent semantic analysis in 1997 already used high-dimensional representations to study words, texts, and knowledge acquisition. Second, representing relationships among language samples is not the same as fully measuring a person's consciousness. Unspoken experience, bodily sensation, emotion, and motivation do not become fully known merely because a model produces a vector. [Landauer and Dumais on latent semantic analysis](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/350/2008/readings/Landauer-Dumais.pdf)

The cognitive space I propose should therefore begin with material we can work with: statements, explanations, choices, and relevant circumstances that people voluntarily provide. We can record and analyze them to build approximate models of particular cognitive relationships. We must test whether the dimensions mean what we think they mean, whether measurements are repeatable, and whether conclusions survive a change of model or language. An internal axis of one model cannot simply be declared humanity's universal axis of justice or civilizational advancement.

### How cognitive frames take shape

People's worldviews, theories of knowledge, political leanings, moral beliefs, and ways of understanding occupy different positions and follow different tendencies across dimensions of thought and action. These differences have histories: personal experience, environment, access to information, and the influences to which a person has been exposed. A view does not arise from nowhere. Nor does it become absolutely correct merely because it is mine.

In this sense, I think cognition that begins with one's own experience can be examined within a broader evolutionary picture. A system capable of sensing and acting needs to distinguish what matters to it and what affects its continued existence, then extend its understanding through interaction. Whether some version of this is a basic feature of every system capable of evolution and emergence remains a question to investigate case by case. Human experience alone cannot establish a law for the entire universe.

If we regard present language models as high-dimensional representations of human linguistic knowledge, we can picture language and action within this cognitive space by analogy with movement through physical spacetime. This is an image of movement and change, not an assumption that the two obey the same equations. Different cognitive frames can create distance, but explanation can also build trust. Interactions among people with different frames then generate more complex structures and properties within the wider frame of society and civilization. Those structures, in turn, affect individuals by shaping the information they encounter and the habits and judgments they develop.

Two things are happening at once: we change our descriptions of the world, and we change the world through action. Someone who understands another group as an enemy may refuse communication. That refusal makes misunderstandings harder to correct and changes the actual possibilities for cooperation. A social model therefore needs more than static coordinates for opinions. It must track changes in information, action, resources, and rules over time. This is why the book later moves from semantic objects to a civilization considered as a running system.

### Relativity does not abolish facts or responsibility

If understanding begins from different positions, does that mean nothing can be right or wrong, good or bad?

What I oppose is the habit of treating one's own cognitive frame as an absolute standard, declaring everything inconsistent with it mistaken, and then turning other people into inherent enemies or demons. But rejecting the substitution of one's own position for a universal standard does not imply that all factual judgments are equally reliable or all actions equally acceptable.

We can understand the circumstances in which someone developed a fear while correcting the factual judgment that fear produced. We can explain why someone harmed another person while still stopping the harm, providing redress, and establishing responsibility. Explaining how an action arose and allowing it to continue are different questions.

Consider a dispute over a public facility. One person sees easier transport; another faces noise, displacement, or higher living costs. Calling the first progressive and the second selfish obscures the problem. Calling the first exploitative and the second righteous can do the same. Record who gains convenience, who bears the costs, and what alternatives exist. The disagreement can then move from opposing identities toward questions that can be investigated.

Even with adequate information, however, real conflicts of interest may remain. Translating two people's words cannot make a limited resource satisfy every demand at once. We still need shared rules, comparison of alternatives, protection of basic rights, and arrangements for compensation. Relativity can help reveal the structure of disagreement. It does not solve allocation by itself.

### Bringing moral judgment back to evidence and shared rules

Human thought and behavior should be open to observation, investigation, recording, and analysis, just as natural phenomena are. Where measurement permits, we should also attempt quantification and modeling. Mystification, sanctification, demonization, and emotional labels should not close off further inquiry.

Poetry and fiction can give us a gentle breeze, yielding grass, sacred light, or demonic darkness. Such language has literary and emotional value. But a scientific account of light cannot replace an explanation of its propagation with the claim that darkness is evil. We should bring the same discipline to social inquiry. Declaring a person or institution sacred cannot exempt it from evidence; declaring an opponent evil cannot remove the need to understand how that opponent came to act as they do.

This does not require people to have no emotions, or public speech to contain no rhetoric. Fear, anger, compassion, and hope are themselves real phenomena worth understanding. What we must avoid is treating them as untested causal conclusions, or as grounds for denying someone the chance to explain, challenge, or participate. Political action affects real people. One group's sense of sacred purpose cannot stand in for another group's consent and safety.

We can still uphold basic commitments to preventing harm, equal participation, and personal autonomy. But we should state their scope, explain how conflicts among them will be handled, identify who interprets them, and allow revision. The identity of the rule-maker cannot be the final proof. Someone who rejects much of my worldview can still test a fact with me or honor a cooperative agreement. That offers a more practicable foundation than requiring everyone to inhabit the same inner world first.

### Turning mathematical terms into usable structures

Vectors, tensors, objects and morphisms, duality, symmetry, fixed points, maximization, and minimization can all supply tools for inquiry. Listing them together will not create a new science. Whenever we use one, we need to say what it refers to, what operations are permitted, what relationships those operations preserve, and how we would discover that the concept does not fit.

|Mathematical concept|A possible use in social inquiry|Questions that must be answered|
|---|---|---|
|Dimensions and vectors|Describe needs, resources, judgments, or risks through several quantities in a specified task|How is each quantity measured, in what units, and with what omissions? A vector is not a whole person.|
|Tensors|Represent multidimensional relationships with specified transformation properties after defining the relevant spaces|Not every multidimensional table has the mathematical properties implied by calling it a tensor.|
|Objects, morphisms, and categories|Treat knowledge objects, states, or protocols as objects, and permitted transformations as morphisms|Can transformations be composed? Are there identity transformations? Does composition satisfy the stated rules?|
|Symmetry and relativity|Test whether relevant judgments remain consistent when names, units, or representations change|Which changes merely redescribe something, and which alter circumstances, rights, or facts?|
|Duality and complementary aspects|Study correspondences between structured descriptions, or connections between knowledge and intelligence, data and programs|A mathematical duality needs a definition. Two related concepts do not automatically establish a duality theorem.|
|Fixed points, equilibria, and extrema|Describe an update that leaves a state unchanged, strategies that respond to one another, or an objective reaching an extremum under constraints|What are the update, payoffs, and constraints? Stability, effectiveness, fairness, and optimality are different properties.|

For example, suppose two groups want help clarifying a disagreement. We can first specify a task, denote their voluntarily supplied accounts and circumstances by $h_i,c_i$, and use an explicitly versioned representation method $E_i$ to obtain $x_i=E_i(h_i,c_i)$. Here $x_i$ is a representation for this task. It neither defines the person nor measures the coordinates of a soul.

We can then try to construct an interpretive relation $T_{ij}$ that restates one group's account in language the other can understand. The tests can be straightforward. Does the first group recognize its meaning? Can the second now restate it more accurately? Can both propose the same checks for factual claims? If the correspondence is incomplete, record what is missing. If the restatement changes the meaning, retain that failure. Writing down $T_{ij}$ does not make it necessarily invertible, lossless, or endowed with all the properties of a geometric transformation.

Next comes a further question: did better understanding improve actual cooperation? Sometimes clearing up a misunderstanding makes a revised plan possible. Sometimes both sides understand each other perfectly and still lack enough resources to meet their wishes. That calls for negotiation and allocation. Adding model parameters while pretending every conflict is semantic will not solve it.

### From cognitive frames to shared construction

I hope to build a mechanism through which different understandings can be interpreted, checked together, and developed further. It should not be a center that assigns everyone the correct coordinates. A Merkle-DAG can preserve original statements, sources, conditions, versions, and revisions, so that a model's interpretation cannot silently overwrite what someone actually said. Models and interpretations may change while earlier statements and disagreements remain recoverable.

Shared records do not require every private experience to be made public. If an authorized summary, local computation, or limited disclosure can solve a problem, there is no need to demand a whole life history. As cognitive models become more capable, we need greater clarity about who may use them, for what purpose, and how the people represented can correct them or withdraw.

This leads to a more concrete question about cooperation, conflict, and social structure. Can people with different knowledge, needs, and preferences retain those differences while building rules for action they can trust together? Relativity helps us abandon the habit of placing ourselves at the absolute center. Shared tests keep us from becoming trapped in worlds that cannot communicate. Institutional construction must then turn understanding into durable cooperation. Connecting those steps is what I seek from a mathematical foundation for social science.

### Alignment begins with a question: aligned with whom?

The discussion of cognitive frames showed how people can inhabit the same world while holding different information, needs, and judgments. Once AI enters this continuing game of social interaction, a frequently omitted question becomes unavoidable. When we say that AI should align with humanity, whom do we mean by humanity?

AI alignment is commonly described as bringing a system's outputs and actions into agreement with human values, intentions, and social norms. For a conversational model, an accessible example is the transition from a base model that continues text to a helpful, honest, and harmless assistant. Learning from human demonstrations and feedback is one practical research approach. But making a model better match the expectations of particular users or evaluators is a long way from resolving society's disagreements over values. [Research on training language models with human feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)

Consider the fact that different peoples, governments, social classes, and communities do not share all the same values, intentions, political rules, or social norms. A consequence follows quite naturally. In humanity's ongoing social game, each player capable of creating or controlling AI—a government, a social class, a company, or an individual—may have an assistant that is helpful, honest, and harmless from its own perspective, yet appears to others as a dangerous accomplice of an opponent.

An AI can execute its client's instructions accurately while shifting losses onto people who had no part in the instruction. A system might improve a firm's negotiating effectiveness, for example, while treating workers' circumstances as irrelevant because success is defined only in terms of the firm's returns. The problem need not be disobedience to the owner. It may be highly effective obedience to a goal that excludes other affected people.

Local alignment therefore cannot simply stand for collective safety. Evaluating a system requires more than checking whether it understood its client's words. What can that client authorize? Whose rights cannot be overridden? Who can challenge the consequences? These questions extend beyond how a conversational assistant answers a prompt. They concern the institutions through which we live together.

### Neither dominance nor a balance of power removes the need for shared rules

As AI capabilities improve and automation extends into research, programming, and experimentation, the actors using these tools may expand their ability to act more quickly. Unequal access to computing resources, data, talent, and infrastructure may allow AI to widen existing disparities.

We should take the possibility of rapid, consequential change seriously. But without a defined task and supporting evidence, we cannot assign a universal ratio in which a lead of a few months necessarily produces a hundredfold or thousandfold difference in capability. Institutional design does not depend on proving a dramatic number. If some capabilities grow markedly faster than our ability to constrain their use and correct mistakes together, we already have reason for concern.

If development is highly uneven and one actor becomes dominant, that actor may see AI-enabled coercion as easier than negotiation among equals. When benefits are assessed only from the dominant party's position, other people's lives and autonomy, future trust, and the creative possibilities lost to civilization may disappear from the calculation.

That does not make coercion necessarily the most rewarding or least costly strategy. Coercion can provoke resistance, degrade information, damage cooperation, and create lasting uncertainty. The earlier discussion of reasoned persuasion and voluntary trials sought another path. The danger here is that, without shared constraints, a local evaluation can reward actions that damage the whole. It is not that every actor with an advantage is destined to choose violence.

Nor does more balanced development settle the problem. Several powers may face one another with comparable capabilities while mistrust, inadequate communication, and rapid action allow a passing thought or minor misunderstanding to escalate toward a catastrophe for civilization, even without a strong initial intention to cause harm. Each may simply want to avoid falling behind, yet keep taking actions that intensify the others' fear. Anxiety about nuclear confrontation during the Cold War helps illustrate this structural danger. AI operates differently from nuclear weapons, however, and its particular risks require particular analysis.

Dominance and confrontation are thus two risk pathways worth studying, not an exhaustive pair of inevitable futures. Parties can establish communication, verification, limits on external harm, and joint procedures for handling accidents. They can retain competition and disagreement while reducing irreversible escalation. What needs to change is the assumption that threatening one another is the only route to safety.

### A civilization swinging a chained hammer in each hand

The earlier image of a child swinging a chained hammer can be extended to the problem of alignment. Consider the adversarial aspects of AI competition between China and the United States. It resembles a creature with two brains, one directing each hand, and each hand swinging a heavy hammer on a chain—without an effective mechanism for coordinating the two.

The left brain sees the right-hand hammer accelerating and concludes that its own hammer must move faster to avoid injury. The right brain reaches the same conclusion. Both hands increase their strength and speed without checking their trajectories together. Each acts in the name of self-protection, yet the hammers may collide or their chains become entangled, injuring the body they share.

The analogy highlights interdependence and a failure of coordination. It does not suggest that a country has a single will, or that China and the United States are the world's only participants. Each contains different people and organizations; other countries and ordinary people also bear the consequences. Precisely because those affected extend far beyond a few decision centers, the rules cannot be settled privately by those holding the hammers.

A better outcome is not to break the other half of the body, or permanently subordinate one brain to the other. It is to make shared dangers verifiable: which actions create them, what information needs to be exchanged, how errors can be recognized, when action must stop, and how correction can occur without being treated as surrender. Strength can continue to grow, but coordination must grow with it.

### Alignment among people, and between people and AI

At a broader scale, people sometimes imagine humanity as a single player and AI as another, fearing that self-awareness will turn an assistant into a tyrant that enslaves or destroys us. Earlier chapters distinguished consciousness, objectives, and behavioral reliability. Humanity likewise cannot be treated as a player whose objectives and conduct are already unified.

In my view, we can no longer avoid alignment among human organizations and individuals themselves. How can different values, intentions, and norms be brought under shared constraints on actual outputs and actions, so that pursuing one's own goals does not casually undermine another person's basic conditions of survival and autonomy?

This does not require identical tastes, faiths, occupations, or ambitions. What needs alignment first is the framework for cooperation and the relationship between promises and actions. We can disagree about the best life while agreeing not to force one another to live it. We can compete to solve a problem while preserving results and failures for others to examine. We can dispute a proposal while protecting the basic rights of the person who questions it.

Better institutional coordination among people gives human–AI alignment a more substantial foundation. Who may set a goal, who will be affected, whether authorization can be withdrawn, who bears the costs, and how disputes are resolved no longer remain hidden behind the relationship between a model and its client. Cooperative AI research likewise identifies improving the shared circumstances of people and machines, and of multiple agents, as an explicit research direction. [Open Problems in Cooperative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.08630)

Yet a shared foundation does not automatically solve technical problems. Goals can be expressed badly, feedback can be misunderstood, and systems can fail in unfamiliar conditions. Even sincere cooperation requires tests of whether a system acts within its authority, can be stopped, and can recover when something goes wrong. Institutional coordination among people and technical alignment between people and AI need to support one another and advance together. Neither can wait for the other to be completed once and for all.

### What would it mean to model alignment as a fixed point?

When I suggest that alignment might be understood as a fixed point, I am asking whether repeated observation, action, feedback, and revision can produce a form of coordination that does not continually push participants toward harming one another.

To turn that idea into mathematics, we must first specify the object that remains unchanged and the transformation acting on it. A reward function ordinarily maps states and actions to an evaluation, as in $r_i(s,a)$. Its inputs and outputs need not belong to the same space. The phrase “a fixed point of the reward function” is therefore not, on its own, a well-defined model.

One possibility is to collect participants' evaluation rules, action strategies, and cooperative protocols into a state $z$. We then define an update rule $F_e$ that revises those components in response to evidence and feedback, with $e$ representing temporarily fixed environmental conditions:

$$
F_e:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z},\qquad z_{t+1}=F_e(z_t),\qquad F_e(z^*)=z^*.
$$

Now $z^*$ is a fixed point of that update rule. If we are specifically concerned with revisions to reward evaluation, we could instead denote a collection of evaluation functions by $R$, define an update operator $U$ on that same function space, and ask whether $U(R^*)=R^*$. This is a modeling proposal that must be constructed and tested. It proves neither that such a point exists in actual society nor that every starting condition leads to it.

A fixed point carries no guarantee of fairness. An institution may remain unchanged because vulnerable people cannot speak, or because erroneous information keeps confirming itself. The coordination we seek must satisfy conditions such as basic rights, opportunities for challenge, and the ability to revise. We must also examine its response to disturbance. Existence, stability, and legitimacy are separate requirements.

A Nash equilibrium asks whether a participant would benefit from changing strategy alone, given the others' strategies. Pareto optimality asks whether someone can be made better off without making anyone else worse off. Maximization and minimization require specified objectives, constraints, and costs. These concepts answer different questions. They do not become a single conclusion merely because each can involve some sense of no further change. Tit for tat, meanwhile, is a particular strategy of response, not a theorem guaranteeing an optimal outcome.

The real world also produces new objects, technologies, and needs; the environment $e$ changes. A more practical aim may therefore be an evolving path that continues to meet shared constraints, allows local experiments, and corrects mistakes in time. Alignment should keep common development possible, rather than lock civilization permanently into a point or forbid its evaluative rules from ever changing.

### Beyond humanity and AI: the conditions that sustain us

Looking further ahead, the new civilization formed by humans and AI must coordinate its activities with the Earth and, eventually, with the wider environments it enters. This is the longer-term direction I mean by alignment.

Humanity has faced the prospect of widespread destruction from nuclear weapons and now faces climate change arising from accumulated patterns of production and consumption. The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Synthesis Report identifies human activities as the cause of global warming. If we fail to examine the wider consequences of civilization's actions, AI may accelerate and enlarge existing patterns of damage. [IPCC Synthesis Report](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/)

Ecological alignment does not mean that Earth or the universe has a single will waiting to be read, or that a universal reward function has already been given to us. It means bringing energy use, material cycles, ecological limits, and effects on other life and future generations into decisions and feedback. An action that looks profitable while leaving irreversible losses to those without a voice cannot readily be counted as progress for civilization as a whole.

Alignment, then, is more than a model giving a satisfactory answer in one conversation. It concerns relationships among individuals and organizations, between people and AI, and between civilization and the conditions of its existence. Tests at one level cannot substitute for tests at another, but they must connect: how goals are formed, how information is obtained, how power is constrained, how outcomes are recorded, and how mistakes are repaired. The discussions of shared knowledge, dynamic decision weights, and institutional self-revision seek structures through which that full sequence can gradually become practicable.

### Keeping relativity open to tests

Extending the idea of reference frames into cognition and society can generate useful questions. It has not yet produced an empirically established social theory of relativity. We must examine separately whether we are redescribing the same fact, changing environmental conditions, investigating how people understand the world, or proposing rules for living together. These questions connect, but no single answer settles them all.

Semantic vectors are representations shaped by materials, training methods, and tasks. They are not complete measurements of consciousness. A feasible small experiment could ask willing participants to explain the same disagreement independently, then compare ordinary restatement with model-assisted restatement. Does misunderstanding decrease? Is the original meaning preserved? Do the results hold on material not used to construct the method? The record must also include cases where the model is unhelpful, mistaken, or obscures a real conflict of interest. A shorter vector distance does not itself demonstrate greater fairness, trust, or safety.

Likewise, calling cognitive differences curvature, trust parallel transport, or a change of perspective a functor provides, at most, suggestive metaphors unless the objects, relationships, and testable structures are defined. Mathematical terminology cannot supply a proof for a model that has not been constructed. The aim should be to make relationships among descriptions open to examination, rather than place people in coordinates that look precise but cannot be challenged.

### Evidence for stable alignment and for continuing correction

Representing alignment as a fixed point of an update operator is a research proposal. It needs a state space, permitted updates, environmental assumptions, participants' rights, and criteria for success. Existence, convergence, recovery after disturbance, and compliance with shared constraints each require their own proof or experimental assessment. A durable structure of domination is a counterexample to the inference that stability means goodness.

A starting point could be cooperation over resources at a small scale. Compare agents optimizing their own local scores with agents operating under shared limits on harm, public commitments, and correction procedures. Test both under imperfect information, unequal capabilities, and changing resources. Record the distribution of gains, incidents of loss, time to repair, effectiveness of withdrawal, and total costs. Retain counterexamples involving refusal to cooperate or collusion. Simulations can help choose further experiments; they cannot establish that a mechanism can safely be applied to the entire world.

Coordination among people can help clarify AI's objectives and authority, but it cannot replace technical safety tests. Ecological constraints likewise cannot be represented solely by scores that current human participants happen to endorse. The common foundation sought by Nova Principia should make these gaps clearer, failures easier to expose, and correction easier to continue. Giving the problems a shared name is not grounds for declaring them solved.
